description: We are a two-member interdisciplinary team with the two members studying physics, software development and artificial intelligence. We aim to use NASA's NISAR satellite data to explore environmental changes in the Bin El Ouidane–Tadla region, focusing on water surface changes and surrounding agricultural landscapes. Our goal is to transform complex satellite observations into an accessible interactive platform that makes local environmental changes easier to visualize and understand.
summary:
Backscatter is a web app that uses NASA’s NISAR radar to watch the water and fields of the Beni Mellal-Khenifra region in Morocco. Radar sends its own signal and reads the echo, so it sees through clouds and at night. Our pipeline cleans nine NISAR images from 22 June to 20 October 2026 and measures three things.

Lake surface. The Bin El Ouidane reservoir lost 1.53 km² of water surface between 22 June and 26 September.
Land types. The region is sorted into six types. Our water class covers 99.0% of the water seen in a cloud-free satellite photo.
Change. What got brighter or darker between any two dates.

Claude writes a plain-language explanation from those numbers, and code checks every number and date before the app shows it. When the signal shifts for reasons the land can’t explain, as it did in October, the app flags it instead of reporting it as change.

This matters because the region depends on scarce water and irrigation. Farm insurers, sugar companies, water agencies and irrigation offices need regular, reliable checks on fields and water. Free radar data can now answer their questions every 12 days.
details:
Live app:

https://interpixel-bm.github.io/Backscatter/

---



What it does and how it works

Backscatter shows the water and fields of the Beni Mellal-Khenifra region of Morocco as seen by NASA’s NISAR radar. NISAR’s L-band radar sends its own signal and measures the echo. Rough surfaces like plants and buildings send back a strong echo; calm water sends back almost none. Because it does not need sunlight, it works through cloud and at night, and it passes over the same place every 12 days.

The pipeline:

  1. Download a window of about 83 × 86 km (20 m pixels) from nine NISAR dates, 22 June to 20 October 2026, all from the same orbit track so they compare fairly.
    • the outline of the Bin El Ouidane lake on each date;
    • six land types found by our own clustering model (open water, built-up, trees and slopes, changing fields, rough ground, smooth ground);
    • what got brighter or darker by more than 3 dB between any two dates.
  2. Explain. Claude writes a short plain-language text from the measurement file only, never from the images.
  3. Check. A script compares every number, date and word limit in each text with the measurements. Only texts that pass are published (135 of 135).

The app shows the maps, a time slider, charts per area and these texts for three preset areas: the lake, the Tadla irrigated plain, and Beni Mellal city.

Benefits

  • Works whatever the weather, every 12 days, from free NASA data.
  • Plain words instead of radar jargon.
  • Every number traces back to a data file.
  • Doubtful dates stay visible. In October, buildings got brighter by up to 2.13 dB, and buildings don’t change. The app flags those dates instead of calling it land change.

Intended impact

The region depends on scarce water for irrigation. A water agency could aim inspections at fields that keep growing while canals are off. An irrigation office could see what each water release produced. A farm insurer or a sugar company could check parcels without visiting every farm. Anyone could watch the lake shrink or refill.

Tools

  • Data: NASA NISAR L2 GCOV radar via ASF and CMR; HLS Sentinel-2 optical images (22 Sep 2026) to check our results.
  • Processing: Python in a conda environment with GDAL, rasterio, pyproj, NumPy, SciPy (k-means) and Pillow.
  • App: TypeScript with Vite, MapLibre GL JS for maps and Chart.js for charts.
  • AI: Claude for the texts, plus a number checker we wrote in plain Python.
  • Hardware: a standard laptop. No paid cloud services.

What is creative

  • The AI cannot invent numbers. It reads only the measurements, and code rejects any text with a number that isn’t in them.
  • Buildings as a ruler. Built-up areas should look the same on every date, so when they shift, we know the image changed, not the land.
  • A fix for a radar trap. At L-band, dry bare fields look as dark as water, so a simple “dark = water” map marked up to 38% of the window as water. We count instead how often each pixel belongs to the lake across the nine dates. With that fix, our water class covers 99.0% of the water seen in a cloud-free photo.

Factors we considered

  • Fair comparison: one orbit track, the same pixels on every date, and averaging done in power before converting to dB.
  • Data gaps: NISAR has no images between 27 July and 10 August; the app says so.
  • Honesty: flags and limits are shown, not hidden.
  • No API keys in the app; texts are generated ahead of time.
  • New areas without code changes: areas come from a config file.
  • Business model: the maps stay free for anyone; organisations pay for answers on their own parcels.
